arguments.content:
In the United States, overall cancer survival has improved substantially over the past few decades — the 5-year relative survival rate for all cancers combined is now roughly 68–70%, up from about 49% in the mid-1970s. Survival varies enormously by cancer type and stage at diagnosis: many common cancers caught early (prostate, thyroid, melanoma, breast) now have 5-year survival rates above 90%, while cancers that are typically detected late (lung, liver, pancreatic) remain far more lethal.

Uncommon cancers (new US cases per year, ascending):
- Adrenal cortical carcinoma: roughly 200–500 cases per year
- Merkel cell carcinoma: about 2,500 cases per year
- Cholangiocarcinoma (bile duct cancer): about 8,000 cases per year
- Anal cancer: about 10,000 cases per year
- Small intestine cancer: roughly 11,000–12,000 cases per year

Deadliest cancers by 5-year survival rate (most to least deadly):
- Mesothelioma: approximately 10–12%
- Liver cancer (hepatocellular carcinoma): approximately 20%
- Esophageal cancer: approximately 23%
- Brain and central nervous system tumors: approximately 26%
- Lung cancer: approximately 28%
